# Leviticus 25:1–28: research notes for a verse-by-verse commentary

**Scope:** I read Enduring Word (Guzik), Ellicott, Precept Austin, Matthew Henry, Benson, the Pulpit Commentary, Haydock, Coffman, Bible Odyssey, New Advent, Catholic Answers, and pages from TGC and Bible Hub. I found nothing usable on Wesley's notes, the Lutheran sites, OCA (Orthodox), the NET Bible notes, or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage, so those are left out.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Guzik says this setting shows Israel was still camped at Sinai. They stayed there from Exodus 19 through Numbers 10. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- Ellicott takes "Mount Sinai" to mean the mountainous region around Sinai. He thinks the chapter belongs with the festival laws of ch. 23 and has been moved, because "there is no strict sequence in the Law." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the laws were given in faith. Israel was not yet in the land, so they would have to trust God to provide enough in six harvests to carry them through the seventh. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- Ellicott: the seventh day honours God as Creator, and in the same way the seventh year honours Him as owner of the land. He also reports the Second Temple-era view that the law took effect in Israel's 21st year in Canaan, after seven years of conquest and seven of dividing the land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html
- Allan Mosley (quoted on Precept Austin): this Sabbath is "to the LORD." The land, the harvest and the rain are not gods. He contrasts the Canaanites' fertility gods and warns modern believers against worshipping possessions. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_25_commentary

**vv. 3–5**
- Guzik: the rule covered both grain and fruit crops. It was a "radical demonstration" that the land belonged to God, not to Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- Ellicott: "sabbath of rest" literally means "a sabbath of sabbaths." He lists later Jewish rules on what counted as cultivation. For v. 5 he notes that "untended vine" is literally "thy Nazarite vine," a vine set apart to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html
- Benson: all the year's farm work stopped in the seventh year, just as daily work stopped on the seventh day. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/leviticus-25.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia says the main purpose of the Sabbath year was to teach that the land was the Lord's and the people were His tenants. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/13289a.htm

**vv. 6–7**
- Ellicott: the produce was for eating, not for trading or storing. It was left in the field for the poor, servants and others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html
- Benson: "the sabbath of the land" means the crop that grew by accident that year. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/leviticus-25.html
- Guzik:
  - Resting the soil was good land management.
  - Matthew Poole thought the Sabbath year put everyone in the place of the poor, and so taught compassion.
  - Israel's failure to keep these years set the length of the Babylonian exile (Lev 26:34; 2 Chr 36:20–21).
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- The Catholic Encyclopedia: what people did not use was left to cattle and wild animals. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/13289a.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: these are seven "weeks" of years. On the Second Temple-era reckoning, the first Jubilee fell in Israel's 64th year in the land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html
- Chuck Smith compares the count to Pentecost: seven Sabbaths, then the fiftieth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-15.html
- TGC's Daniel commentary sees this counting behind Daniel's "seventy sevens" (Dan 9:24), which it calls a tenfold Jubilee. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/daniel/

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the horns were rams' horns. The point of sounding them on the Day of Atonement is that God had just forgiven Israel's debts, so each Israelite should forgive his debtors. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html
- Guzik quotes Adam Clarke: liberty was announced only on the day of atonement, which suggests that gospel redemption had to wait for Christ's sacrifice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- Sermons collected on Bible Hub make the same point: the Jubilee came only after atonement (W. H. Jellie), and the Gospel age is the world's Jubilee, begun by Christ's atonement (A. G. Brown). https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/25-28.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott:
  - "All its inhabitants" means the Israelites. The ancient authorities therefore held that the Jubilee lapsed once the Transjordan tribes were taken captive.
  - *Yôbel* means both "ram's horn" and its sound.
  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html
- Guzik:
  - Rooker notes that even the slave who chose to stay with his master was freed at Jubilee.
  - The verse is inscribed on the Liberty Bell.
  - There is little Old Testament record of the Jubilee being kept.
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- The Pulpit Commentary finds two purposes in this verse: proclaiming liberty, and every man returning to his own property. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-25.html

**vv. 11–12**
- Ellicott: the 49th year was a Sabbath year and the 50th the Jubilee, so the land lay fallow two years running. Food was taken straight from the field each day as needed, not stored. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html
- Guzik quotes Rooker: two fallow years in a row "would have been a severe test of faith." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- The Catholic Encyclopedia: anyone, including the owner, could eat the crop, but only for immediate use. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08534a.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik:
  - The holdings returned were the family allotments of Joshua 13–21, so no family stayed landless for ever.
  - He also applies the verse to believers, who will hear a trumpet (1 Thess 4) and come home.
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- James Smith (quoted on Precept Austin): what was lost in Adam is restored in Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_25_commentary

**vv. 14–16**
- Ellicott:
  - "Oppress" is better rendered "overreach."
  - Later Jewish law let an overcharge of more than a sixth cancel the sale.
  - Buying land was like buying the rest of a lease, and the fallow years were left out of the price.
  - The seller sold a number of harvests, not the land itself.
  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html
- Henry: buyer and seller must deal at fair value, knowing the land will return, and must discount the Sabbath years. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_025.cfm
- Guzik: this was not socialism. Only land was redistributed, and the system kept Israel from developing a permanent underclass. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: fear God, because He takes up the cause of the oppressed and avenges injustice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html
- Knox's translation on New Advent renders the verse as warning of "a divine vengeance to reckon with." https://www.newadvent.org/bible/lev025.htm

**vv. 18–19**
- Ellicott: by obeying, Israel would have the security other nations try to win with armies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html

**vv. 20–22**
- Ellicott:
  - He compares this to the double manna given before the Sabbath (Ex 16).
  - The worry is really about the eighth year.
  - He thinks vv. 20–22 logically belong after v. 7, and may have been placed here because they also cover the Jubilee.
  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-25.html
- Guzik: the promise was so sure that God said He would "command" the blessing. He links it to Matthew 6:33. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- One Precept Austin note says a three-year crop (not two) shows the Jubilee was planned for as well. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_25_commentary

**v. 23**
- Guzik: all the earth is the Lord's, but He claims this land in a special way. Believers today are also "strangers" (1 Pet 2:11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- Henry: selling one's share of the land would in effect cut a family off from fellowship with God. That is why Naboth refused to sell his vineyard. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_025.cfm
- Clarke: Israel was God's tenant. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/leviticus/25-23.html
- Coffman: being a sojourner is the true status of all people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-23.html
- Maclaren: the law tended to prevent extremes of wealth and poverty. https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/25-23.htm

**vv. 24–25**
- Clarke: the kinsman is the *goel*, "redeemer," a picture of Christ, who took on human nature in order to become our kinsman. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-25.html
- Henry: Christ is the one kinsman able to redeem (compare Ruth 4). Some also take the verse to mean Christians should restore those who have fallen. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_025.cfm

**vv. 26–27**
- Haydock (Catholic): if a buyer paid 100 and had already received 80 in value, the seller repays 20. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-25.html
- R. Reid: the seller pays for the use of the land for the years left until the Jubilee. https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/25-23.htm

**v. 28**
- Coffman: if redemption fails, the Jubilee still restores the land. Christ, our near kinsman, gives back our lost inheritance. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/leviticus-25.html
- A sermon on Bible Hub: the land came back without payment, a picture of Christ recovering what sin had forfeited. https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/25-28.htm

---

## 2. Where interpreters differ

The pages rarely name their denomination. Coffman's StudyLight page is labelled Restoration Movement / Arminian; the other commentators are named but not labelled. So I can show real disagreements between named teachers, but I couldn't confirm that they line up with denominations.

**v. 8 / v. 10: Is the Jubilee the 49th or the 50th year?**
- Henry thinks the 49th year is most likely, called "the fiftieth" by a common way of speaking. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_025.cfm
- Benson insists on "precisely the fiftieth." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/leviticus-25.html
- Hawker leans toward the 49th. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/leviticus-25.html

**vv. 10–13: What does the Jubilee point forward to?**
- *Israel's future.* Gaebelein sees Israel's coming restoration and the millennium, and calls a universal "restitution of all things" reading unscriptural. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_25_commentary
- *Two stages.* TGC's commentary says the Jubilee began with Christ (Luke 4) but is fulfilled in two stages matching His two comings. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/leviticus/
- *The Gospel age now.* Coffman calls the Christian era "earth's Jubilee." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/leviticus-25.html

**Does the law apply today?**
- Guzik: some principles would bless modern society, but not all can carry over. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- A TGC Themelios article: Paul does not tell Christians to keep the Sabbath or Jubilee years, but God's mercy should move us to show mercy. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/leviticus-in-light-of-christ/

---

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- Bible Odyssey (vv. 9–10):
  - Leviticus assumes a spring New Year, so the autumn horn in the 49th year probably announces a 50th year starting the next spring.
  - Selling land became in effect leasing.
  - The release did not cover non-Israelite slaves, so there was "no general abolition of slavery."
  
  https://biblehub.bibleodyssey.org/articles/jubilee-year/
- A TGC survey article reports Israel Knohl's view that this material comes from a time of social division (Hezekiah's era) and was meant to counter it. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/pentateuchal-studies-today/

**Was it ever kept?**
- Guzik quotes Harrison: the evidence is lacking, though Jeremiah 34 records an attempt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- Haydock reports that the Jubilee lapsed after the exile while the Sabbath year continued. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-25.html

**Catholic**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia sees the Jubilee as a model: on the Day of Atonement, people forgave each other's debts as God forgave theirs. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08534a.htm
- Catholic Answers links Leviticus 25:10 to Isaiah 61 and Luke 4. https://www.catholic.com/tract/year-of-jubilee-catholic-answers-guide-to-jubilee-2025
- John Paul II said Jesus fulfils the Jubilee tradition. Citing vv. 8–12, he urged reducing or cancelling the debt of poor nations. https://www.newadvent.org/library/docs_jp02tm.htm
